publication.title: Towards a childcare guarantee
publication.locator: Table S.1, printed page 7 (PDF page 7); repeated as Table 1, printed page 25

source_table: Table S.1: Estimated costs of a reformed childcare subsidy scheme
source_column: Subsidy level 1 (families not in receipt of means-tested benefits) 75%, subsidy level 2 (families in receipt of means-tested benefits) 95%: Cost
note: Table note: 'IPPR costings based on current market rates and take up. Analysis assumes complete rollout of 30 free hours for all children between six months and four years. The earnings cap is expected to have a negligible effect on costs'. IPPR and Save the Children's Delivering a childcare guarantee (December 2022) says the 60% version 'would cost £2.7 billion (not accounting for current spending)' (printed page 22) and '£2.7 billion per annum in total – with and estimated £1.6 billion recouped from current spending on the childcare element of universal credit and the current tax free childcare scheme' (printed page 34), so Table S.1's costs are read as scheme totals; IPPR states this of the 60% row only. The scheme covers school-age children too. Geography: the report sets out 'a new vision for childcare in England'; Table S.1 states none, and Tax-Free Childcare is UK-wide. The report states no year; Table S.1's sources are Coram Family and Childcare (2022), DWP (2021) and ONS (2021; 2022c). 2022-23 is staged as the price and policy base of a report published in September 2022, not as a year IPPR states.
pe_missing: IPPR's figure is the total cost of one subsidy replacing both Tax-Free Childcare and the UC childcare element (95% for UC families) and covering school-age care, in a world with 30 free hours for every child from six months, at 2022 rates. The analysis publishes the change in spending from replacing Tax-Free Childcare alone with a 75% subsidy, keeping the UC element at 85% and the 2025 entitlements, in 2027-28 to 2029-30. Its results file also holds the reform's spending on the subsidy (legs.subsidy.spending.tax_free_childcare, 5.5062 in 2027), which the dashboard does not publish and which leaves out UC families; neither figure measures IPPR's quantity.

conditions.basis: with a childcare-use response (Model 1), before any labour market response
conditions.comparison: net additional cost against the fully expanded funded hours system

reform_hint: Universal core provision of 15 hours a week, free for all children from nine months to four years old ... For working families, a cap on childcare costs as a percentage of family earnings (we propose 5% but we also model for 7.5% to demonstrate the impact on costs) for hours purchased above this core provision to enable them to work.

publication.title: The Universal Family Childcare Promise: Guaranteeing support for parents and children
publication.locator: Summary, printed page 2 (PDF page 2); repeated on printed page 8

source_column: Net additional cost to the government as usage expands, current provider rates
quote: At current hours of usage our proposed system would initially be cost-neutral, but as usage expanded it would present a net additional cost to the government of ~£3-3.4bn (based on current rates paid to providers, which we believe need to be reviewed regardless of the system in place) compared to the fully expanded funded hours system.
note: Printed as one range, '~£3-3.4bn', staged as its two ends. 'Current rates' are the 2025/26 government rates of Table A.2 (printed page 23); the period is that price base, not a year in which the cost falls: 'Any expanded system would not cost the full amount presented immediately, as it would take time for families to respond to the new offer' (printed page 18). The model is built on the 2022-23 Family Resources Survey. Printed page 18: at current reported hours the system 'costs an estimated £27m more to £331m less than the funded hours-based system', rising to 'a net additional cost of £3.0-£4.1bn a year more for our system under Model 1 (assuming no labour market response)' across its 5% and 7.5% caps and current and 10%-higher provider rates; printed page 8: net additional costs 'decline by as much as 11.4% once dynamic estimates of potential labour market response are accounted for'. The analysis lists this costing in its own comparable_costings as the closest published analogue to its free-hours leg.
pe_missing: NEF's figure is the net cost of replacing the whole system (the funded hours, Tax-Free Childcare and UC childcare support) with 15 universal hours from nine months plus an earnings cap on further hours, once families buy more childcare. The analysis keeps the working-parent 30 hours and the UC element, lets no childcare use respond to the 75% subsidy (results file subsidy_take_up.note: 'Neither models new childcare use'), treats 90.53% of new free hours as displacing care families already buy (assumptions.free_hours_displacement), and publishes no figure on NEF's definition.
